titles.to: Oak Wood, Ash Wood, Birch Wood

replace.find: Eglė was the youngest of twelve sisters. Twelve, as my mother had twelve brothers. In that house the linen never dried and the soup pot never cooled. The sisters rose before sun and carried their shifts and sashes down to the lake, for it was washing day and the sky was clear.
replace.with: Eglė was the youngest of twelve sisters, and there were twelve brothers besides. In that house the linen never dried and the soup pot never cooled. The sisters rose before sun and carried their shifts and sashes down to the lake, for it was washing day and the sky was clear.

replace.find: The sisters clutched each other. The mother crossed herself after the old way, thumb to forehead to earth. The father took up his axe.
replace.with: The sisters clutched each other. The mother touched thumb to forehead and then to earth, after the old way. The father took up his axe.

replace.find: She took her red sash and tied it tight. She put on her wreath, though the rue had wilted. She kissed her mother. She kissed each sister in turn, twelve kisses, salt on her lips. The house smelled of smoke and sour milk and fear. Outside the frogs sang in the ditch as if nothing were wrong.
replace.with: She took her red sash and tied it tight. She put on her wreath, though the rue had wilted. She kissed her mother. She kissed each sister in turn, eleven kisses, salt on her lips. The house smelled of smoke and sour milk and fear. Outside the frogs sang in the ditch as if nothing were wrong.

replace.find: Eglė walked three days from the lake to the sea with the snakes for company. You know how this goes. The black road moved and hissed around her feet. At night they ringed her while she slept, scale to warm scale, and the moss smelled of rain and cold mushrooms. In the morning they brought her bilberries on broad leaves. She ate and walked on. Her red sash grew dusty. Her wreath of rue shed its dry leaves one by one along the path.
replace.with: Eglė walked one long day from the lake to the sea with the snakes for company. The black road moved and hissed around her feet. At noon they ringed her while she rested, scale to warm scale, and the moss smelled of rain and cold mushrooms. They brought her bilberries on broad leaves. She ate and walked on. Her red sash grew dusty. Her wreath of rue shed its dry leaves one by one along the path.

replace.find: On the third evening they came to the dunes. The wind stood up and pushed at her shawl. Gulls cried high and thin. The sand was white and stuck between her toes, and the sea lay before her, grey green and wide as the sky turned over.
replace.with: At evening they came to the dunes. The wind stood up and pushed at her shawl. Gulls cried high and thin. The sand was white and stuck between her toes, and the sea lay before her, grey green and wide as the sky turned over.

replace.find: On the first morning of the tenth summer my father parted the water. You know how this goes. He lifted his staff and the sea stood up on two sides like walls of green glass. Fish hung shining in those walls. Gulls cried far above where the sky showed through.
replace.with: On the first morning of the tenth summer my father parted the water. He spoke his three old words and the sea stood up on two sides like walls of green glass. Fish hung shining in those walls. Gulls cried far above where the sky showed through.

replace.find: We walked three days from the sea to the lake. You know how this goes.
replace.with: We walked one long day from the sea to the lake, dawn to dusk.

replace.find: First day through dunes where grass cut our ankles and amber lay after storms. My brothers filled their pockets. I found one piece small as a pea and held it tight till it warmed.
replace.with: First through dunes where grass cut our ankles and amber lay after storms. My brothers filled their pockets. I found one piece small as a pea and held it tight till it warmed.

replace.find: Second day through pine woods where resin smelled sharp and the ground was soft with needles. We drank from springs with our cupped hands. Cold. So cold it made our teeth ache.
replace.with: Then through pine woods where resin smelled sharp and the ground was soft with needles. We drank from springs with our cupped hands. Cold. So cold it made our teeth ache.

replace.find: Third day through rye fields where men stopped their scythes to stare. A woman carrying flax crossed herself and then smiled at my mother's red sash. Village dogs ran out and sniffed our sea smell and sneezed.
replace.with: Last through rye fields where men stopped their scythes to stare. A woman carrying flax touched her brow and then the earth, and then smiled at my mother's red sash. Village dogs ran out and sniffed our sea smell and sneezed.

replace.find: On the evening of the third day we saw the lake.
replace.with: At evening we saw the lake.

replace.find: The eldest uncle looked at Azuolas. He set down his netting needle.
replace.with: The eldest uncle looked at Ąžuolas. He set down his netting needle.

replace.find: Azuolas looked at Uosis. Uosis grinned and tossed a pinecone at him. Berzas held my hand. I held Berzas sleeve because my own hands shook too much to hold anything rightly.
replace.with: Ąžuolas looked at Uosis. Uosis grinned and tossed a pinecone at him. Beržas held my hand. I held Beržas sleeve because my own hands shook too much to hold anything rightly.

replace.find: Go on, said the youngest uncle. He is not yet bearded but his smile made room for you. We will keep the little ones safe.
replace.with: Go on, said the youngest uncle. He was not yet bearded, but his smile made room for all of us. We will keep the little ones safe, he said.

replace.find: So Azuolas went. Just like that. The eldest uncle tall beside him, an axe on his belt that clinked when he walked. They went past the rye field where the stalks hissed in wind. Past the sauna where birch smoke curled. Into the oak wood where the light fell green and broken.
replace.with: So Ąžuolas went. Just like that. The eldest uncle tall beside him, an axe on his belt that clinked when he walked. They went past the rye field where the stalks hissed in wind. Past the sauna where birch smoke curled. Into the oak wood where the light fell green and broken.

replace.find: They were gone past midday. When they came back the uncle's face was red. Azuolas walked straight. His shirt stuck to his back with sweat. A scratch bled thin on his cheek from a low branch. He sat down and drank cold milk in long swallows and said nothing about the wood.
replace.with: They were gone past midday. When they came back the uncle's face was red. Ąžuolas walked straight. His shirt stuck to his back with sweat. A scratch bled thin on his cheek from a low branch. He sat down and drank cold milk in long swallows and said nothing about the wood.

replace.find: Azuolas wiped his mouth with his hand. He looked at me steady.
replace.with: Ąžuolas wiped his mouth with his hand. He looked at me steady.

replace.find: Nothing, said Azuolas. I showed him an acorn. I told him oaks keep their leaves long.
replace.with: Nothing, said Ąžuolas. I showed him an acorn. I told him oaks keep their leaves long.

replace.find: That night my mother braided my hair and sang. She did not ask where Azuolas had been. The fire crackled and threw sparks up to the stars. The men were quieter than the night before. An owl called once from the oak wood and Azuolas did not look up.
replace.with: That night my mother braided my hair and sang. She did not ask where Ąžuolas had been. The fire crackled and threw sparks up to the stars. The men were quieter than the night before. An owl called once from the oak wood and Ąžuolas did not look up.

replace.find: Two uncles came for Uosis after the midday meal. The flour armed one and the one with the child on his shoulders the day before. They carried baskets for mushrooms and a small knife each.
replace.with: Two uncles came for Uosis after the midday meal. The one with flour on his arms, and the one who had carried a child on his shoulders the first evening. They carried baskets for mushrooms and a small knife each.

replace.find: Uosis loved any game. He took a basket too big for him and swung it till it hit his knees. He looked back at us and crossed his eyes to make Berzas laugh. Berzas laughed through his nose and milk came out and the women clucked.
replace.with: Uosis loved any game. He took a basket too big for him and swung it till it hit his knees. He looked back at us and crossed his eyes to make Beržas laugh. Beržas laughed through his nose and milk came out and the women clucked.

replace.find: They kept him till the light went low and long across the linen. When they came back the baskets were half full and Uosis sang a farm song wrong and loud. The uncles laughed but their eyes did not laugh. The flour armed one kneaded his hands together as if dough still stuck there.
replace.with: They kept him till the light went low and long across the linen. When they came back the baskets were half full and Uosis sang a farm song wrong and loud. The uncles laughed but their eyes did not laugh. The flour-armed one kneaded his hands together as if dough still stuck there.

replace.find: I told them ash bends and does not break, he said. I told them I lost the path and found mushrooms. He rolled over. His voice went small. Drebule. My throat hurt from holding shut.
replace.with: I told them ash bends and does not break, he said. I told them I lost the path and found mushrooms. He rolled over. His voice went small. Drebulė. My throat hurt from holding shut.

replace.find: I put my hand on his back and felt him breathe. My own throat ached in answer. I wanted to tell him he was brave as Azuolas. The words stuck like burrs. I patted instead, clumsy, till he slept.
replace.with: I put my hand on his back and felt him breathe. My own throat ached in answer. I wanted to tell him he was brave as Ąžuolas. The words stuck like burrs. I patted instead, clumsy, till he slept.

replace.find: Three other uncles took Berzas in the afternoon. They did not ask so much as lift. Come, little apple cheek, they said. The birch wood has sap sweet still if you know where to tap. We will show you how your mother drank as a girl.
replace.with: Three other uncles took Beržas in the afternoon. They did not ask so much as lift. Come, little apple cheek, they said. The birch wood has sap sweet still if you know where to tap. We will show you how your mother drank as a girl.

replace.find: Berzas went glad because an uncle held his hand on each side. His feet barely touched the ground between them when they swung him over a ditch. He looked back and waved with his whole arm. I waved back with fingers that fluttered like leaves.
replace.with: Beržas went glad because an uncle held his hand on each side. His feet barely touched the ground between them when they swung him over a ditch. He looked back and waved with his whole arm. I waved back with fingers that fluttered like leaves.

replace.find: I envied Berzas most of all. Azuolas had steadiness. Uosis had laughter. But Berzas had tears that brought women running with honey cake. He had a softness men carried gently over ditches. I had only shaking that spilled sap and stammering that made even kind men look away to spare me.
replace.with: I envied Beržas most of all. Ąžuolas had steadiness. Uosis had laughter. But Beržas had tears that brought women running with honey cake. He had a softness men carried gently over ditches. I had only shaking that spilled sap and stammering that made even kind men look away to spare me.

replace.find: They were gone a shorter time. When they came back Berzas rode on an uncle's shoulders with a birch bark crown crooked on his head. His cheeks were wet. Whether from sap or crying I could not tell. He slid down and ran straight to my mother in the hayfield and buried his face in her skirt. She stroked his head and looked over him at her brothers.
replace.with: They were gone a shorter time. When they came back Beržas rode on an uncle's shoulders with a birch bark crown crooked on his head. His cheeks were wet. Whether from sap or crying I could not tell. He slid down and ran straight to my mother in the hayfield and buried his face in her skirt. She stroked his head and looked over him at her brothers.

replace.find: That night Berzas would not eat honey though the youngest uncle offered it on his knife tip. He sat close to Azuolas and Uosis on the bench and the three made a wall with their shoulders. I sat a little apart because my shaking rattled the bench and Uosis put his foot on mine to still me, kind and heavy.
replace.with: That night Beržas would not eat honey though the youngest uncle offered it on his knife tip. He sat close to Ąžuolas and Uosis on the bench and the three made a wall with their shoulders. I sat a little apart because my shaking rattled the bench and Uosis put his foot on mine to still me, kind and heavy.

replace.find: Later in the loft Berzas cried without sound. His shoulders jumped. Azuolas put an arm round him. Uosis put an arm round him from the other side. I lay outside their knot and put my hand on Berzas ankle where it stuck out, thin and warm, and held on.
replace.with: Later in the loft Beržas cried without sound. His shoulders jumped. Ąžuolas put an arm round him. Uosis put an arm round him from the other side. I lay outside their knot and put my hand on Beržas ankle where it stuck out, thin and warm, and held on.

replace.find: Berzas shook his head against the straw. The straw rustled. The linen smelled of sun going cold.
replace.with: Beržas shook his head against the straw. The straw rustled. The linen smelled of sun going cold.

replace.find: The youngest uncle stayed behind in the yard. He was not old like the eldest. His beard was thin and yellow. His hands were quick with snares and whistles. He sat on the chopping block and turned something small between his thumb and finger. It caught what little sun there was.
replace.with: The youngest uncle stayed behind in the yard. He was not old like the eldest. His chin was still bare, with only yellow down along the jaw. His hands were quick with snares and whistles. He sat on the chopping block and turned something small between his thumb and finger. It caught what little sun there was.

replace.find: Drebule, he said. Come. You need not run after the boys today.
replace.with: Drebulė, he said. Come. You need not run after the boys today.

replace.find: My name in his mouth stopped my feet. He had never said it before. The others called me little one or sister's last or not at all. He said it plain, Drebule, as if it were easy on the tongue.
replace.with: My name in his mouth stopped my feet. He had never said it before. The others called me little one or sister's last or not at all. He said it plain, Drebulė, as if it were easy on the tongue.

replace.find: Drebule, he said. You are a good girl to come. Your brothers are strong trees. Oak holds. Ash bends. Birch weeps but holds. You are the youngest. The smallest. No one expects the hard thing from you.
replace.with: Drebulė, he said. You are a good girl to come. Your brothers are strong trees. Oak holds. Ash bends. Birch weeps but holds. You are the youngest. The smallest. No one expects the hard thing from you.

replace.find: Say it once more plain, he said, and leaned closer. His beard brushed my cheek. It smelled of smoke.
replace.with: Say it once more plain, he said, and leaned closer. His hair brushed my cheek. It smelled of smoke.

replace.find: Good girl, he said. Good Drebule. He patted my shoulder twice. Now run back before rain comes. Say nothing of our walk. It is our secret, bead girl.
replace.with: Good girl, he said. Good Drebulė. He patted my shoulder twice. Now run back before rain comes. Say nothing of our walk. It is our secret, bead girl.

replace.find: In the yard my brothers were playing knucklebones by the door. Azuolas looked up. Uosis grinned with a bone between his teeth. Berzas moved over to make room for me in their line.
replace.with: In the yard my brothers were playing knucklebones by the door. Ąžuolas looked up. Uosis grinned with a bone between his teeth. Beržas moved over to make room for me in their line.

replace.find: Where were you, Azuolas said.
replace.with: Where were you, Ąžuolas said.

replace.find: On the sixth day my mother mended nets by the lake. The flax smelled of sun and damp. Midges sang above the water. My brothers skipped flat stones and I counted their skips and said nothing of the alder hollow. The bead lay in my pocket and burned.
replace.with: On the sixth day my mother mended nets by the lake. The flax smelled of sun and damp. Midges sang above the water. My brothers skipped flat stones and I counted their skips and said nothing of the alder hollow. The bead lay in my pocket and burned. The yard was quiet that day. The twelve uncles had gone before light to cut hay in the far meadows, they said, and they came home after dark with sea sand on their feet and said little at supper.

replace.find: Drebule, she said. Little grey eyes. You told. You shall tremble as you trembled. Be aspen. Shake in fair weather and foul. Whisper without rest what you told in alder shade.
replace.with: Drebulė, she said. Little grey eyes. You told. You shall tremble as you trembled. Be aspen. Shake in fair weather and foul. Whisper without rest what you told in alder shade.

replace.find: Hush, she said, and laid her palm upon my crown. It was warm from sleep nine years gone, from plaiting my hair that morning. Sleep under my hand a moment. Then wake and shake.
replace.with: Hush, she said, and laid her palm upon my crown. It was warm, as it had been every night of nine years under the sea, as it had been that morning plaiting my hair. Sleep under my hand a moment. Then wake and shake.

notes: Restored Lithuanian diacritics (Ąžuolas, Beržas, Drebulė) through ch4-6; made the sea one day's walk (ch2-3) and sent the uncles to the shore on day 6 so Žilvinas's death fits the timeline; removed Christian crossing from pagan setting; youngest uncle stays beardless; staff to spoken words; eleven kisses; retitled ch3-6. Left the brief's 'nine years old' vs born-in-year-six age gap and the white-then-red foam.

replace.find: On the moss bed the lamia lay laboring. Not Andere Urgorri who had knocked, but her sister, younger, her gold hair stuck to her neck, her duck feet restless against the moss. Andere knelt by her and held her hand and sang under her breath.
replace.with: Andere Urgorri lay down on the moss bed and labored, her gold hair stuck to her neck, her duck feet restless against the moss. Her younger sister knelt by her and held her hand and sang under her breath.

replace.find: The work was long but it was clean work. The lamps burned blue. The river breathed outside. At last a cry rose, thin as a kid goat, and the child was born and wailing, with a head of damp gold and feet like its mother. Kattalin wrapped it and laid it on its mother's breast. The mother laughed and wept. Andere Urgorri pressed her brow to Kattalin's hand.
replace.with: The work was long but it was clean work. The lamps burned blue. The river breathed outside. At last a cry rose, thin as a kid goat, and the child was born and wailing, with a head of damp gold and feet like its mother. Kattalin wrapped it and laid it on its mother's breast. The mother laughed and wept, and pressed her brow to Kattalin's hand.

replace.find: From a stone table she brought bread. Ah, that bread. Round and dark crusted, still warm, smelling of the oven and of childhood. It smelled like Kattalin's mother's kitchen sixty years gone, onion and rye and woodsmoke. Kattalin's stomach spoke. Her knees ached from kneeling. She had not eaten since noon soup.
replace.with: From a stone table the sister brought bread. Ah, that bread. Round and dark crusted, still warm, smelling of the oven and of childhood. It smelled like Kattalin's mother's kitchen sixty years gone, onion and rye and woodsmoke. Kattalin's stomach spoke. Her knees ached from kneeling. She had not eaten since noon soup.

replace.find: Kattalin took the three coins and slipped them in her apron pocket. She took the comb for the new mother, to comb the babe's hair when it grew.
replace.with: Kattalin took the three coins and slipped them in her apron pocket. The comb she left for the new mother, to comb the babe's hair when it grew.

replace.find: The sister lamia lifted her head. "Ask a favor in return for the favor," she said. "It is our law. We pay every debt."
replace.with: The sister lamia spoke up. "Ask a favor in return for the favor," she said. "It is our law. We pay every debt."

replace.find: No cock would crow for an hour or more. Dawn far. The bridge would be finished. Peio would lose his soul for love of his wife, which is a high price and a common one. The lamiak would collect, for they pay every debt and collect every debt. That is their nature, not cruelty. A cat is not cruel for catching mice.
replace.with: No cock would crow for hours yet. Dawn far. The bridge would be finished. Peio would lose his soul for love of his wife, which is a high price and a common one. The lamiak would collect, for they pay every debt and collect every debt. That is their nature, not cruelty. A cat is not cruel for catching mice.

replace.find: From the next farm came another cock, waked by the first. Then another down the lane. Then the priest's fine white cock. Then every cock in the valley, crowing in the dark, in the rain, an hour before dawn, shouting at nothing.
replace.with: From the next farm came another cock, waked by the first. Then another down the lane. Then the priest's fine white cock. Then every cock in the valley, crowing in the dark, in the rain, hours before dawn, shouting at nothing.

replace.find: Her basket banged against her knee. Linen, scissors, thread, dried yarrow. Gold coins sewn tight in her pocket slapped her thigh. Her belly was empty. She had not eaten the lamia bread, and good that she had not, for a mouthful would have bound her seven years in the cave. Old law. Everyone knows it. Still, the smell of that bread followed her, warm and wheaten, like her mother's kitchen on baking day.
replace.with: Her basket banged against her knee. Linen, scissors, thread, dried yarrow. Gold coins in her apron pocket slapped her thigh. Her belly was empty. She had not eaten the lamia bread, and good that she had not, for a mouthful would have bound her seven years in the cave. Old law. Everyone knows it. Still, the smell of that bread followed her, warm and dark with rye, like her mother's kitchen on baking day.

replace.find: "Gau on," she said. "Good evening to the work."
replace.with: "Gau on," she said. "Good night to the work."

replace.find: Then Andere spoke. Her voice was even. Laminas do not shriek like market wives. That is for humans.
replace.with: Then Andere spoke. Her voice was even. Lamiak do not shriek like market wives. That is for humans.

replace.find: She nodded to her sisters. Two of them slipped down the arch like otters, light for all their burden. They found a great oak beam on the bank, left by the flood, and dragged it up. Wood scraped on stone. The sound set Kattalin's teeth on edge. They laid the beam across the gap at the crown. It spanned from finished stone to finished stone, narrow, wet, bouncing a finger's width when touched.
replace.with: She nodded to her sisters. Two of them slipped down the arch like otters. They found a great oak beam on the bank, left by the flood, and dragged it up. Wood scraped on stone. The sound set Kattalin's teeth on edge. They laid the beam across the gap at the crown. It spanned from finished stone to finished stone, narrow, wet, bouncing a finger's width when touched.

replace.find: "Less talk," Kattalin said, taking back her basket from where Andere's sister had set it gently on the bank. "Where is she?"
replace.with: "Less talk," Kattalin said, untying the basket from her arm and taking up her lantern, which one of Andere's sisters had carried over the arch and set gently on the bank. "Where is she?"

replace.find: "In the house. My mother is with her. The water is in the lower field. We moved the goats." He talked fast, tripping on words. "I promised them, ama. I stood here at dusk and shouted and they came. I said take my soul if the bridge stands. I did not think. She screamed and I—"
replace.with: "In the house. Her mother is with her. The water is in the lower field. We moved the goats." He talked fast, tripping on words. "I promised them, ama. I stood here at dusk and shouted and they came. I said take my soul if the bridge stands. I did not think. She screamed and I—"

replace.find: Near the end Maialen cried out, loud, and Peio burst in though his mother pushed at him.
replace.with: Near the end Maialen cried out, loud, and Peio burst in though Maialen's mother pushed at him.

replace.find:
Once there was a midwife waked at midnight, and if you had been there you would have heard it too.

Toc, toc, toc at the door. Not loud. Patient as rain.

Kattalin Irazabal sat up in bed with her heart walking fast. The fire was low. The wind pushed at the shutters. She took her lantern and opened, and the wet night breathed in her face.

A tall woman stood on the step with water shining on her hair. Gold hair down to her knees, combed smooth, dripping. A green gown that smelled of the river. A face sorrowful and lovely. Under the hem, where feet should be, flat webbed feet like a duck in the mud.

You know how this goes. You have heard it at other hearths.

Come, the lamia said. My time is on me.

Kattalin put on her clogs. She took her basket of clean linen. She took her lantern in the rain and went where she was led, down to the cave behind the fall where the water talks all night. Inside the cave the air was warm as breath and smelled of moss and milk. On a bed of dry moss the lamia laboured, her comb set aside, her hair spread wide.

Kattalin did her work as she does for Christian women and for others. She spoke low. She waited. She caught the child cleanly when it came, a girl child with wet gold down on her head, lungs strong as a lamb. She tied and cut, washed in warm water from a copper pot, wrapped in linen from her own basket.

Then the lamia, whose name was Andere Urgorri, the Red Lady, rose up shining and set out bread on a stone. Eat, midwife, she said. And here is gold for your hands.

The bread steamed. It smelled like Kattalin's mother's bread from when she was small, crust dark and the crumb close. Her stomach turned over with hunger and tiredness. Her mouth filled. For the smell alone she near wept.

But the old rule stood in her like a lintel stone. Never eat what a lamia offers, or seven years you bide with them under the hill.

Kattalin took the gold. She left the bread.

From the cave mouth, while she washed her hands in the stream, she saw them. Sisters in green gowns hauling stones in moonlight, singing without words, building. An arch rising over the black water stone by stone. Duck feet slapping wet rock. Gold hair flying.

For Peio Arrieta across the flood, Andere said, combing her hair again. His wife cries out in labour and no cart can cross. He spoke fair and plain. His soul if the bridge stands by cockcrow.

And across the river, thin through rain and water noise, came the cry. Maialen in her pains. Peio's wife. The bridge still lacked its last stone, the crown stone that locks the arch.

So Kattalin did what you know. She ran in her heavy clogs to Peio's own farm, to the dark henhouse where the hens shifted and muttered. She shut herself in with the smell of droppings and warm feathers. She threw back her head in the dark and crowed like a rooster with all her widow's breath. Kikiriki. Kikiriki. Kikiriki till her throat bled.

And every cock in the valley woke and answered, farm to farm, till the bargain broke on a false dawn. That is told already.
replace.with: Once there was a bargain spoken twice in one night, and if you had been there you would have heard the rain go quiet to listen.

notes: Cut ch3's replay of ch1 (which contradicted it: Peio's henhouse, Andere as mother); made Andere the labouring lamia in ch1 so ch2-3 'my daughter' holds; fixed crowing time, Peio's vs Maialen's mother, basket/lantern after the crossing, sewn coins, rye bread, 'Laminas', Gau on gloss; retitled duplicate ch3 and ch2. Left ch3's unquoted dialogue style.

replace.find: She got out and crouched by the ruts. The soil held the tread marks, a closed lorry, wide tyres. Alentejo mud caked in the grooves, already baked hard by noon. Joaquim bent beside her, knees cracking, and touched the edge with the back of his hand.
replace.with: She got out and crouched by the ruts. The soil held the tread marks, a closed lorry, wide tyres. Alentejo mud caked in the grooves, already baked hard by noon. Joaquim lowered himself beside her, one hand on his knee, and touched the edge with the back of the other.

replace.find: Tiago had said white, closed, no lights. Three in the morning past the cafe. The brakes at the crossing.
replace.with: Tiago had said white, closed, no lights. Three in the morning past the cafe.

replace.find: They drove on. The track joined the paved road past the water tank. The tank smelled of iron and pine needles in the heat. Rosaria counted the stripped rows as they passed, red trunks flashing between green crowns. Sixty wounds drying in the sun.
replace.with: They drove on. The track joined the paved road past the water tank. The tank smelled of iron and pine needles in the heat. Red trunks flashed between the green crowns as they passed.

replace.find: She led them to the scale. Fifty nine planks lay in a pile, still sweating sap, pores deep and clean. The outer faces bore the estate mark. Rosaria laid her palm flat on the top plank. Cool despite the sun. The cut underneath was smooth where the wrist had twisted right.
replace.with: She led them to the scale. Fifty nine planks lay in a pile, still sweating sap, pores deep and clean. Flecks of white paint showed on the outer faces, the broken tails of painted 7s. Rosaria laid her palm flat on the top plank. Cool despite the sun. The cut underneath was smooth where the wrist had twisted right.

replace.find: "I sent an estimate request," Henrique said. His voice shook. Sweat shone on his chin under the trimmed beard. "I owed you. I never said steal. I deleted the messages because— because I was ashamed for my father to see."
replace.with: "I sent you the file because you said you knew buyers," Henrique said. His voice shook. Sweat shone on his chin under the trimmed beard. "I owed you. I never said steal. I deleted the messages because— because I was ashamed for my father to see."

replace.find: Outside the cicadas rang off the tin roof. The younger guard chalked the fifty nine planks as held and took the papers from the manager. Old Leitao answered the phone on speaker, his voice rough through the static, and when the guard said the bark was found he went quiet a long moment.
replace.with: Outside the cicadas rang off the tin roof. The younger guard chalked the fifty nine planks as held and took the papers from the manager. The woman guard called the estate on speaker.
